llm_major: No Korean paper evaluates intrinsic tokenization metrics against downstream performance: the correlation evidence is Turkish (10.48550/arxiv.2502.07057), European (10.48550/arxiv.2310.08754) and English (10.48550/arxiv.2404.13292), and 10.48550/arxiv.2105.09680 (KLUE) and 10.1587/transinf.2017edp7085 (Sejong) never link tokenization metrics to downstream results.

Korean-specific vocabulary design (size, composition, monolingual vs multilingual) is effectively unanswered: the conditional vocabulary claim rests on Turkish (10.1145/3578707) and European (10.48550/arxiv.2310.08754) studies, and the Korean items are an ASR corpus (10.3390/app10196936), a multi-language OOV paper (10.2197/ipsjjip.29.490) and a report that gives no efficiency numbers (10.48550/arxiv.2402.14714).
llm_minor: The conditional claim that whitespace handling is 'task-dependent' rests on a single sentiment-only study (10.3390/electronics10070845), which cannot show task dependence.

The vocabulary-size conditional merges two unrelated findings (larger vocabularies help morphological tokenizers in Turkish, and multilingual tokenizers need about 3x vocabulary for European languages) into one moderator statement, and neither involves Korean.

The EEVE/Chinese-LLaMA consensus claim implies encoding-efficiency gains for Korean, but the EEVE abstract (10.48550/arxiv.2402.14714) reports no efficiency numbers, and it compares '2B tokens' of data with '20,000 tokens' of vocabulary as if they were the same quantity.

The cross-language cost-disparity consensus cites 10.48550/arxiv.2310.08754, which studies tokenizer effects on training cost and performance in European languages and does not show API cost, latency or context loss for under-served languages.

The morpheme-vs-subword conflict compares different contrasts (morpheme+BPE vs BPE in 10.48550/arxiv.2010.02534, standalone Mecab-Ko vs SentencePiece in 10.1080/08839514.2023.2175112) and omits 10.3390/electronics10070845, which also found subword units more robust than morpheme units.
The first gap's factorial design (4 vocabulary sizes × 2 initializations × 2 freezing schedules × 3 budgets = 48 runs) does not match its stated compute of about 20 runs.
The morpheme-vs-subword gap cites the KLUE benchmark paper (10.48550/arxiv.2105.09680) as evidence, but it contains no tokenization comparison.

llm_major: rq4 has no Korean paper linking intrinsic tokenization metrics to downstream scores: 2502.07057 is Turkish, 2310.08754 is European, 2404.13292 is English-centric, and KLUE (2105.09680) and the Sejong study (1587/transinf.2017edp7085) never connect tokenization metrics to downstream results, so the sub-question passes the count check but is effectively unanswered.

rq3 is answered for Korean only by tangential papers: an ASR corpus (3390/app10196936), a multi-language OOV study (2197/ipsjjip.29.490) and an EEVE report without efficiency numbers (2402.14714), while the vocabulary-size evidence is Turkish (1145/3578707) or European (2310.08754), so the effect of Korean vocabulary size and composition on sequence length and performance is not actually answered.
llm_minor: The third consensus claim merges three different tagging studies (2197/ipsjjip.29.490 on OOV in transfer learning, 1145/3591206 on spacing-robust POS tagging, 1162/089120102317341774 on a 2002 unknown-morpheme tagger) and attributes '97-98 points' to both spacing errors and unknown morphemes, although each paper tested only one and they are tagging results rather than tokenizer comparisons.

rq6 asks about noisy user-generated text, but the only direct Korean evidence is review sentiment (1080/08839514.2023.2175112) and OOV robustness in 3390/electronics10070845; spacing evidence comes from POS tagging, so noise handling by tokenizers is thinly covered.

The vocabulary-design gap states that Korean vocabulary design is 'unstudied', which overclaims since absence from this 23-paper table does not show absence from the literature, and the cited evidence ids (1145/3578707, 2310.08754, 3390/app10196936) are non-Korean or ASR papers.

The rq5 consensus on vocabulary extension rests on a single Korean technical report (2402.14714, leaderboard only) and a Chinese study (2304.08177), and no cited paper evaluates generation quality or Korean inference cost, which the sub-question explicitly asks about.
